utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Jordash, are you ready to continue your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Further Cross-examination by Mr. Jordash: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a few remaining questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, before we do so. Mr. Vujovic, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony, that is, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Jordash, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have on the screen, please, P3162.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to just very quickly return to the subject of the financial reward which the Prosecution say demonstrates your affiliation --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which the Prosecution say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all unnecessary microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the document again, and I wanted to ask you whether you recognised the signature there, and look particularly at the second name, the surname. Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very hard for me to see who signed this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the first name there be Dragisa?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It says "Deputy Chief," and that was Mr. Dragisa Ristivojevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was Mr. Stanisic's second deputy, with the first one being Tepavcevic?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Mr. Stanisic had two deputies. The first one was Milan Tepavcevic, and the other one was Dragisa Ristivojevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Ristivojevic, is this right, was the deputy in charge of operatives?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was how things were officially. Mr. Milan Tepavcevic was the first deputy and Mr. Dragisa Ristivojevic, as the second deputy, had a lower scope of duties, and he was in charge of operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if that signature is Ristivojevic's, would that be consistent with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, is there dispute about that this is not Mr. Stanisic's signature?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that was clear already yesterday, Mr. Jordash. So unless there is any specific reason why it's so important to establish whose signature it was, but apparently it's a deputy, not Mr. Stanisic, who signed the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think the deputy that my learned friend indicated did not exist was in relation to another document, which is a signature which we say was Tepavcevic's. But unless I missed something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm wrong, but here apparently there is no dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Then I can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to -- perhaps we can move back into public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in public session but the document was not to be shown to the public and has not been shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I've finished with the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just returning to the issue of your resignation or your replacement, you said yesterday that the straw that broke the camel's back was when Rade Markovic was brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honours, page 19721.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was his being brought in to replace Stanisic the straw that broke the camel's back?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not that last straw as him. But what he told us at the first collegium meeting as the future course that the service was going to take, what he stated at that moment and why I said that that was the last straw was that we were supposed to continue working normally, that until further notice we would remain in our posts. He said that, obviously, there would be some personnel shakeups, and that he expected from all of us - and let me quote - "loyalty to the president, the state, and the party."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were flabbergasted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Am I correct that Markovic came from the public security so had no experience of state security business or limited experience, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic was an officer in the Serbian police, in the public security, and his deputy, who had been appointed, Mr. Nikola Curcic was also employed by the public security, never by the state security. He was also 80 per cent disabled, and he was appointed as the chief of sector. The motives of those who decided on those appointments must have been specific, otherwise he would not have appointed a person who had been involved in a car accident and ended up disabled. So the two leading men that were appointed at the time had joined from the public security sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise for interrupting. On line 12, the family name of this person was not properly recorded and I do not see the sign pointing to the fact that this might be corrected subsequently, so I'd like to verify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You earlier spoke about Mr. Nikola, and could you repeat his family name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Curcic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. By the way, Mr. Petrovic, often if it's these kind of technical matters, if you make a small little note and give it to the transcriber and say that you think that it might be wrongly written down, then certainly it will be taken care of. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it correct, from at least where you were standing, but also I suggest it was public knowledge at the time, that Markovic was on friendly terms with the Milosevic family and in particular with Milosevic's son, Marko?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a notorious fact. Although he was a police general by rank, his main activity was to look after President Milosevic's son. That was basically his principal job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without going too much off the subject, and it was also equally notorious that Marko was engaged in criminal activities along with Radovan Stojicic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was what was known, by and large.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, again, Nikola Curcic was also part of Milosevic's inner circle. That, again, was a notorious fact; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. Mr. Curcic was the Milosevic family's friend through his own brother. When Mr. Milosevic was still a banker, the two of them went to New York together, so I believe that they were quite close, the two of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So rather than this being a case of you leaving because of your affiliation with Stanisic, this was a Milosevic purge of the State Security Service and a replacement of key posts by persons who he was particularly close to; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was absolutely the case. You know we worked in very hard times, as a service. We had a very clear concept of the service's role and place in our state system. I personally and intimately and professionally agreed with that concept. Most of us were not going through the motions of the job. We were convinced that we performed the function that Mr. Stanisic defined as the basic task of the service, and that was protect the state, the people, and the constitutional order. All those years that's what we believed in, and all of a sudden there was turmoil and there was a new wind blowing and a new direction -- a new course that we had to adopt, and I did not agree with all that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to complete this subject, it was Markovic who was chief of the service when members of the DB attempted to assassinate Stambolic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, not only did they try to do that but they did kill him. When Mr. Markovic was in charge, all those ugly things happened and there was a ripple effect of all that. If you will allow me just one more sentence. One of Mr. Stanisic's postulates, something that he shared with us often at collegium meetings, was this: "While I am the boss of the Serbian Intelligence Service, the Serbian Intelligence Service will not be involved in political killings," and that was a fact. When Mr. Markovic came and after that a lot of ugly things happened, things that were a stark contrast with the principles that we had adopted and functioned on while Mr. Stanisic was in charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the last question: Markovic was also the chief when Djindjic was assassinated by members of the DB; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic is serving 40 years' imprisonment for something, isn't he? What's that?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because of the killings that happened primarily -- and the murder of Mr. Stambolic and his involvement in that. When prime minister Djindjic was murdered, Markovic was already serving his gaol time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. My mistake. Thanks very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No more questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. Mr. Petrovic, any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, a few.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Further Re-examination by Mr. Petrovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Vujovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us first look at P3161. P3161, under seal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, yesterday my learned friend showed you this list. Let us just briefly look at it again. Under numbers 2, 3, and 4, do you recognise any of the names under these numbers?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zoran Mijatovic under 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document was drafted in September 1993. Could you please tell us what was this gentleman's position at the time?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic was chief of the 2nd Administration or the head of the Belgrade centre. I don't know exactly what his position was in 1993. I suppose that he was chief of the 2nd Administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please look at the last column, the last vertical column. There are some Roman numerals here, and when you look at number 16, 17, 18, where your name is and your associates' names there are also Roman numerals?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Obviously the Roman numerals represent the number of the administration. I was affiliated with the 7th Administration, so were my associates, and I see the Roman numeral VII next to my name there. So this is the 7th Administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the end of the list you can see under 20 or 21 "CRDB Uzice," and then in the last column it says "CRDB Sremska Mitrovica." Do you perhaps have a explanation for these entries under 20 and 21?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this is a document issued by the 8th Administration and it concerns per diems, the only explanation I can provide is that from these centres - and that was common practice - funds were requested for per diems. They provided documentation about their administration, and the 8th Administration just confirmed that Uzice and Sremska Mitrovica had received a certain amount of money that they would then distribute among themselves. In my view this was a normal procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, yesterday my learned friend showed you another document, P3162. This document was about a reward of 2.500 dinars that you got from your superiors. Mr. Jordash has just showed you that document, and my learned friend tried to prove that that showed your inclination towards the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 2D1790. It was uploaded yesterday. It is not in the system. Your Honours, I have hard copies for the Bench and for everybody in the courtroom, the copies in both languages, English and Serbian. So I would like the usher to help me distribute the documents among the participants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I believe this also should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that true, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, the Chamber wonders why we need hard copies of this document? Is there any specific reason for that, because we usually look at documents on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. No, Your Honours, the reason is the fact that we decided to show the document yesterday. We uploaded it in the system, but it hasn't been released. We will not be able to see it on our screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, have you received a copy of this document?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document from your personal file. Could you please tell us the following. It says here in the statement of reasons that the coefficient for your monthly salary for May is being decreased by 20 per cent. Could you please tell us whether a decrease in salary is a form of punishing employees?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, perhaps, what the reasons were for the heads of the service to punish you with this decrease of 20 per cent?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very specific. Something needed to be done. I was late. That was my responsibility. That's why I was punished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This decision was signed by the assistant head of the department of state security. The assistant head is one of the top people in the service, right?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, decreasing one's salary, do you see that as proof of being close to the top echelons of the service or a distance between yourself and the top echelons of the service?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, in my view, reward and punishment is not a question of closeness within a service. At one point in time somebody assesses that they are supposed to reward you, and another point in time their assessment is that you need to be punished. From my point of view, that is all part of the work process and the work discipline that prevailed then in the service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vujovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would kindly ask that this document be admitted once the technical conditions are met.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you already assign a number to this, as I understand, non-released document which already is uploaded into e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. May I just clarify, the number of the document that will be uploaded is 2D1790?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2D1790 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1709 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1709 will receive number D899, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D899 is admitted under seal. Please proceed, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, could we now please take a look at 65 ter 4385.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 4385, Prosecution number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, this is a decision that is identical to the decision that was made in terms of your own punishment. This is a decision punishing Franko Simatovic, special advisor in the state security department at the proposal of the chief of the department. August 1995 is the time involved. Do you know, perhaps, why Stanisic was -- Stanisic punished Simatovic in this particular case?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your understanding of this decision concerning Simatovic's punishment in view of his position in the service, special advisor, and this punishment is being meted out? How do you explain that in terms of the functioning of the service at the time?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time Mr. Simatovic was a special advisor. When I was punished, I was head of an administration, so I was within the management line. Both show what I've already talked about, that is to say, discipline and work. That was particularly focused on at the time. You would be rewarded for your good work and also you would be punished for your omissions. So that is to say there was hardly any leeway.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could this please be admitted as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 4385 will receive number D900, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Is there any need to have it under seal, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think there is no need for that, but please do allow me to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, just one more question, if you can help us with that. Yesterday in response to the question put by His Honour the Presiding Judge, you tried to explain to us how much 928 million dinars was in September 1993. Could you please explain that to us. What was the situation in the financial system of Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at that point in time, the autumn of 1993, the time of these millions and billions?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the simplest possible terms, if I were to say that we had a bank note, a bill, of 5 billion dinars, so daily inflation at that point in time was over 10 per cent per day. So all of these figures were skyrocket high. Millions, billions. I don't know. A kilo of sugar cost like 2 and a half million or something like that. Those were crazy times as far as this inflation was concerned in Serbia, that year, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vujovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, if it goes in the millions and the millions, of course that can only happen in a situation of inflation. What I was interested in was what, on the day this document was signed, the approximate value of that was in Deutschmarks. That there was inflation is not really something you could even think of not being there. Any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question so that I perhaps try to explain what you asked about, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, in the autumn of 1993, how often did the value of money change?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On a daily basis, quite literally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that means, "on a daily basis"? For example, what was the percentage during the course of one day?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For instance, if you were supposed to have 10 Deutschmark exchanged, at 10.00 a.m. there would be one exchange rate and it would be completely different at 4.00 p.m. It would be two times less, for instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, the witness said 10 per cent a day, and now two times less, that's a hundred per cent. That is a contradiction. Either we are able to establish what the approximate value was or we are not, but to further explain how inflation works in such an economy, that is not assisting -- at least is not assisting me and perhaps also not my colleagues. Please proceed if you have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vujovic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, I beg your pardon. May I just pick up on one small issue. It's one I accidentally missed out in my re-examination. It won't take more than two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I look at the clock, and Ms. Friedman has patience, isn't it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I am grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps more even than I have. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Jordash: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A very quick subject which I wanted to clarify, if possible. Yesterday there was a discussion between you and the learned Prosecutor and then the learned Judge concerning your knowledge about what was being monitored from these listening posts. And there are two remarks I wanted to ask you about. Your Honours, page 19688, you said: "Specifically what is being monitored, what is of interest for monitoring in order to be used further, that was decided upon by the intelligence line of work. So they said if Izetbegovic talks to Sacirbey, we are going to monitor that, but we are not going to waste times on other things, equipment or personnel." What did you mean by the comment: "They said ... we are not going to waste time on other things, equipment or personnel"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, could you please verify the page reference, because for me, yesterday, the 23rd, starts in the 19000s and not in 18000s.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, I meant to say 1900 -- sorry, I meant to say 19688.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You appeared -- do you understand my question? You appeared to be making a distinction, and I want to understand what you meant by: "... we are going to monitor Izetbegovic, but we are not going to waste time on other things, equipment or personnel."

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is part of objective reasoning. That is to say, if you are monitoring a spectrum, for instance, of course in the hierarchy of information the most interesting information is the information coming from the very top of a particular setting. Izetbegovic in this particular case. Although, in that area there can be lower-level information, too. Of course, these would be the priorities. They would be monitored and documented. That's very simple.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, as you also said at Your Honours' page 19690, tangible professional success, as you understood it, from the listening posts, was the monitoring of high-level political conversations, as far as the State Security Service was concerned; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Absolutely. That's the way it is. Information that can be obtained by listening to the conversations of high political officials are certainly the most important and of greatest interest, and that's the context that I put it in. I said that when my people came back from the terrain, they simply bragged, if you will, professionally, saying that that had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman, any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please activate your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Further Cross-examination by Ms. Friedman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just on cross-examination you were shown a document -- sorry, re-examination, you were shown a reduction of pay for Franko Simatovic in August of 1995. Are you aware of other members of the service having their pay reduced at the same time?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was rewarding and there was punishing, so your question had to do with other people and my answer is yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in August 1995, to your knowledge, could there have been a deduction due to Operation Storm having taken place?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I don't think so. These were disciplinary measures related to some specific situations. I could not link that punishment meted out to Mr. Simatovic to Operation Storm, that is. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, with your leave, there is just one document that I did not put to the witness that I think perhaps he can help us with that I would like to show him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll find yourself in a similar position as Mr. Jordash --

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- a minute ago. I think that where I expected that you would be very patient, that Mr. Jordash would be now, isn't it. And Mr. Petrovic shares. Mr. Jordash. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Can we have 65 ter 1583.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, this is an organisational chart showing communication between the Serbian MUP, the RSK government, Banja Luka CSB, and then on the bottom level, the locations of secretariats of the interior in the RSK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the characterisation of the document, this is not a communication chart. The document itself says what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's then read what it is, Ms. --

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Correct. Yes. It's an organisational chart displaying -- well, that's what I want to ask the witness about. Apparently direction, circular, and network connections. I don't know if that's -- I presumed it was communication. But that's what I thought that the witness with his experience in electrical engineering and in the federal MUP and the Serbian MUP might be able to help us out with.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could we know who authored this diagram, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: The diagram was produced by the -- from the Croatian archives, the archives from the Republic of Croatia. We can -- in fact the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there are two questions, I think. The one is what the source of the document is, where it was obtained. The other one is - and that was the question, I think, Mr. Jordash put - who is the author who produced it, not in terms of obtaining it but by drafting it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes. The information about the author is -- is unknown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: We only have information about where it was seized.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, are you able to explain what the -- first of all, the meaning of the different kinds of communication -- the different indicators on the bottom, direction, circular, network?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could do that as an engineer who had not dealt with that, though. I've already said that in the State Security Service of Serbia there was a special service that dealt with the system of communications and cryptographic encryption. What you showed to me looks like an organisational chart. What is KZ? That is probably cryptographic communications. And somebody showed here that there was some flow of information that had been encrypted. That's the only thing that I can understand on the basis of this. And purely speaking as an engineer, that would be my interpretation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So which information would you say is encrypted? All the different lines, or only some of them? Is there a way to tell?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say. It really depends on the users involved. It's the user who decides whether he is going to use encryption when sending information or not. I am not in a position to give you an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any -- do you know why -- what the difference is between direction - I think it means direct - the straight bar line, and the network line which is like a dash? Do you know what the difference is?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can mean different things. One of the possible interpretations is that the direction between two points is a particular communication directed a certain way, and then further down there is some kind of network that they can use to communicate between and among themselves. There is nothing else I can say. Once again, I am telling you this as an engineer. I am speaking as an engineer on the basis of something that I would find logical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have any, let's say, educated guess about what information is in the -- or based your knowledge as an engineer, what the information in the circles are, the numbers, 107, 31 -- 0 -- 55?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely do not know what that means.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I inquire as to the relevance to the Prosecution case, since --

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes, the -- and maybe one more question, actually, in case the witness can help us with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to the chart, the Serbian MUP is joined by the direct line to the RSK MUP and by network to the RSK SUPs. So does this mean that if these are different kinds -- lines of communication, that if one is down, let's say the RSK MUP can connect to the Serbian MUP, for the line is okay, then they can get through them to the network?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Objection to the question. Entirely speculative. The witness knows nothing about this, whether this diagram represents any sort of reality whatsoever. So to ask the witness to move from this document, which he doesn't know, whether it represents reality and ask him a question as to what happened in reality is entirely illogical, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think perhaps maybe the question I should ask before is:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you've seen not this particular chart but another similar chart before?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But whether he's seen a chart like this before, to ask him -- well, either ask him in this chart does this mean this, when the witness has said his knowledge is extremely limited, speaking as an engineer what this -- in relation to what this chart means. But then to ask a question which in some way asks him -- is based on a presumption that this represents a reality is entirely speculative. It's -- it's -- it's -- on top of that, this is not, as I understand it, the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's not in the pre-trial brief. It's not a case that they have advanced that somehow the Serbian MUP was involved in assisting the RSK MUP with their cryptographic data protection issues. It's nowhere. It's a late -- it's a late plank to the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber needs more time to consider whether or not this is admissible evidence, yes or no, and also whether it -- if admissible, whether it's most appropriately done through this witness or through the bar table. Therefore, the document will be MFI'd. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1583 will receive number P3164, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. Any further questions or any further matters, Ms. Friedman?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Could I just make a brief submission about the document. I said it was Croatian state archives but it came from the Banja Luka Security Centre. That is one thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is quite a different source. Still the authorship not being resolved by that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any time context which can be -- not when you obtained it but the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Based on -- just based on other evidence, but no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: -- there is nothing more -- perhaps the other documents that were collected at the same time, we could look at that and offer that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not stop you from looking at that, Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And we do -- also in terms of the relevance, it's of course relevant to paragraph 15(1) [sic] of the indictment, the channel of communication. And I can expand on those submissions if ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be best that we have brief written submissions on the matter so that we can look at it a bit more in detail. And I think, as a matter of fact, that the core of arguments would be -- should be possible to write that down in one sheet of paper, and if the other party does the same and really not describing the whole of the history, et cetera, but just give us the relevant information which you think is for relevance, probative value, and reliability, that we have some guidance when further considering this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Should we file them simultaneously or ...? I suppose the objection should be first, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, as a matter of fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I am not sure it should, because if - sorry to detain the Court - but if this is relevant to the allegation that Mr. Stanisic was a channel of communication, then, of course, that allows the Prosecution to rely upon anything that any witness ever says about what Mr. Stanisic ever did which had anything to do with speaking to anyone. It's carte blanche to lead any evidence they want. So it would be useful if the Prosecution actually, having produced this at the close of the case, said what it is it demonstrates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, what is usually the result of saying one party should be first, that if the other party responds, then the first party wants to reply to that again. So why not -- you have your ideas on why it's relevant. Share that view with Mr. Jordash. Mr. Jordash knows exactly what it is that he objects to. And if you exchange that information, then you put on paper knowing what the argument of the other party is, and then the Chamber will be best assisted in deciding the matter. Mr. Jordash, are you willing to share your views with Ms. -- perhaps a cup of tea and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I mean, I've shared my views probably in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's all, then, of course -- Ms. Friedman, if you have shared already all your views with Mr. Jordash, then there is nothing that keeps you from making the submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if not, please share whatever you have not yet shared.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Can I just clarify, then, what the next step Your Honours would like us to take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next step is that you tell each other, cup of tea or cup of coffee, what -- why you think it should be admitted. Mr. Jordash tells you why it should not be admitted. And then you make your submissions in writing, short, compact, and then the Chamber will be assisted by it. What about a time-limit by this Friday?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's good. If you're running out coffee or tea, I have some tea bags and some coffee available.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Can the exhibit be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it has been marked for identification already. Any further matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing further. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, could I just ask the witness one question about the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You may undermine your own position that it should not, but you are certainly aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Jordash: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke as an engineer. Was that because you have not heard or do not know anything about whether this diagram represents reality or not?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have absolutely no information about this. I've already stated several times here in this courtroom that a different organisational unit was in charge of communications. I don't know what the system was like, neither was I interested in that. I was more interested in Croatian communications than our own, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can I just take instructions, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The answer is therefore no, the witness has no knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you confirm - if you can't, you can't - but can you confirm that the State Security Service was not, in fact, engaged in crypto-protection? This was something that was done by the military during the -- during the war?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the organisation of the security system in a state, the military is the main body in charge of encryptic protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was not the question, I think, the witness answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please focus on the question and answer that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you any knowledge as to whether the DB was engaged in crypto-protection? I am not suggesting your department. I am suggesting that the State Security Service was not engaged in crypto-protection. Do you know that or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, have you looked at page 19704, line 5 and following? Especially the first three lines following line 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. Can I just take instructions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether you want to -- yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you did say the other day that the 4th Administration was involved in cryptographic data protection. Do you know anything about how they conducted that?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try and explain. In our state, the army was in charge of crypto-protection, and that's true. The users of crypto-protection were state bodies. The state security department was one of the users, as well as the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. When it comes to the exploitation and the application, the setting up of the equipment, that was done by the communications administration. They did not generate encryption codes. They used what was generated in that centre that was run by the army and that's the whole matter. The whole thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, just one question, please. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the clock, and I had two questions on my mind. Perhaps I put them first and then give you an opportunity to put the last question to the witness. Witness, I would like to take you back to P3160, not to be shown to the public. But waiting for that document, I have another question for you at this moment. When the salary of Mr. Simatovic was reduced in August 1995 by 20 per cent, could you tell us what Mr. Simatovic was engaged in professionally in that month? If you know, tell us. If you don't know, tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Simatovic was special advisor in that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am asking -- what I'd like to know is specifics about his activities during that month. Not his position but where he was, what he was dealing with at that moment, specifically whether he travelled, whether -- detailed -- I mean, what he actually did that month.

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about the tasks at which we co-operated, and that was the organisation of intelligence post. My part of the communication with Mr. Simatovic was within that context, i.e., how to organise all that, which men to send, and so on and so forth. If there were any other tasks, I don't know what those were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say your knowledge was limited to your dealings with Mr. Simatovic in that month. You said it was the organisation of intelligence posts. Which intelligence post you are dealing with in August 1995 in your dealings with Mr. Simatovic? If you know --

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1995 the posts that operated were at Jelova Gora, Pajzos, Brankovac, on Petrova Gora, Pljesevica, those were the intelligence posts that we discussed. There was even a meeting at Pajzos, and I believe that that meeting took place in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I was talking about August 1995. Any specifics about August 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I really can't be that specific. I am sure I can't tell you anything that specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about the reasons, the specific reasons apart from not performing his duties as expected, but any specifics about the reason for the deduction by 20 per cent of the salary of Mr. Simatovic? If you know anything about it, please tell us. If you don't know, tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I take you to P3160. On the map, if you would look at it, we see that the posts in the west, Petrova Gora, Licko Petrovo Selo, and Pljesevica, are relatively close to each other. Would it be logical to say that if you have such listening posts relatively closest to each other, that it would mainly focus on local communication rather than on long-range commutations?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mutual closeness of intelligence posts depends by and large on the geography of the area. For example, if you're operating from a mountainous area, two intelligence posts that are a couple of kilometres away from each other as the crow flies translates to huge differences in the ability to monitor radio waves. That's why the intelligence posts have to be close. And as to your question, an intelligence post is set up in order to monitor a rather limited area, and that's why an intelligence post is located as close as possible to that target area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. They cover a limited area, and therefore you need more. They cover a limited area, but that coverage is related to the limited area of the communications, isn't it? If you are broadcasting something with not much power which would establish communications at a distance not more than 25 or 30 kilometres, you couldn't listen in if you are at a distance of 50 or 70 or 100 kilometres from that place. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you told us several times that it would be interesting to know about communications between Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Sacirbegovic. Now that would be long-range communications, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, if you would want to listen in, you would have to be within the range of that radio communication used by those persons. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, it is -- if we look at Petrova Gora, Licko Petrovo Selo, three relatively close monitoring posts. That wouldn't make much sense if you wanted to monitor the long range. At least you would need only one good one to monitor such kind of long-range communications, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, within that context. Let me explain, however. Licko Petrovo Selo and Pljesevica -- if you will allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pljesevica is a mountain top and the intelligence post was on top of that mountain. And Licko Petrovo Selo was there to receive information from the mountain in order to forward the information to Petrova Gora. I just needed to explain this very specific situation and the closeness of the three points. And for the communications that you have just mentioned, there are systems, as we discussed on the first day of my testimony, when you monitor a radio spectrum you don't have to be that close. If the range of radio waves is short, then the reception abilities are much more comfortable. And you can be quite further away from the target area. So, for example, you could monitor some of the communications on an ultrashort waves even from Belgrade, and that was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if you would like to monitor local communication, for example, between army units which had a very limited range, would you agree that you would need, then, a series of listening posts close to where that -- those army units were operating?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you monitor communications at a lower levels of decision-making, there has to be more intelligence posts. The intelligence posts that we had monitored somewhat higher levels of developments and decision-making, and that's why their numbers were lower than the numbers of those that would have been dependent on some other ambitions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You are taking the question to a matter I didn't ask you. I asked you about local communications. Would you agree with me that if a relatively weak communication sender, well, let's say at a distance of 50 kilometres from Petrova Gora would be used, which, as far as the power is concerned, would have a reach of 30 kilometres, that you would miss it when you are listening in from Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way you described the whole situation, it would be approximately more or less exactly what you have described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that if you want to listen in to communications of the other party, communications with a limited range due to the low power used by the sending equipment, that you would need more listening-in posts in order not to miss part of those short-range communications?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Objectively speaking, that was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have two questions but I am looking at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I am looking at the Stanisic Defence. Two questions, Mr. Jordash, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, to be honest, I -- I found that last section very difficult to follow. It's my fault entirely. And what I would respectfully request is just the break to consider that, because I do see where this might be heading, and I do want to be able to deal with it if it's heading in that direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I ask myself, let me not make a -- I ask myself why you need several posts at short range when you want to listen in what Mr. -- and far away from the place where you would expect Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Sacirbegovic being present, and that's what I asked myself and tried to translate it into objective terms, technical terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's precisely -- I just wanted a short time just to consider that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Because it was my fault I just couldn't follow it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What we will then do is the following. As far as time is concerned - I am also looking at Mr. Stanisic - the two questions of Mr. Petrovic, would that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection at this moment. Because then we could ask the witness to remain standby until after the break and see whether there is any need to put further questions to him. Mr. Petrovic, two questions. Further Re-examination by Mr. Petrovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vujovic, first of all, do you know if in 1994 and 1995 in the area of Petrova Gora and Pljesevica, did the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina have its own surveillance and intelligence posts? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From 1991 to 1995 at the level of the MUP of Serbia, was there a communications administration?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the level of the MUP of Serbia, there was a communications administration in the public service, and there was also a communications administration in the state security. Those were two separate administrations. So my answer is yes, there was a communications administration at the level of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. I'm abusing the fact that you were so short because I had one other question for the witness. Mr. Vujovic, the Chamber received evidence about a long column, where you almost could not see the end of that column, moving to Petrova Gora, which suggests that there were many people involved. Do you know anything about what the activities of other persons in Petrova Gora may have been apart from the technical people which were deployed there on behalf of the 7th Administration? Do you know anything about what the others did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know about the experts of the 7th Administration, and I know about the employees of the intelligence administration, and the two sets of people co-operated. I don't know about anybody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you say there were only people from the 7th Administration and intelligence administration or may there have been others from other administrations at Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sure that there were other people, for example, from the communications administration. It was only logical. But I don't know if there was anybody else, and if there were, who they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now the people you were aware of, you just told us about, in total how many would that have been all together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yesterday when I answered questions I provided an average, but that number changed, and I am only talking about the people I was aware of, people from the technical services, because I was responsible for them. I dispatched them. As for the other groups, how many there were, how many men there were, I really don't know. And if I gave you any figures, that would just be speculation on my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. We take a break. Mr. Jordash is updating his technical knowledge about range of communications, and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I just ask one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. I've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, only one last question to answer. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Jordash: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've now followed what you were saying, so I want to ask you this: If the listening post had been designed to obtain a comprehensive picture of military operations in Croatia and Bosnia, are you able to estimate how many listening posts would have been required?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give an accurate estimate, but it would certainly be more than there had actually been.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are we talking one or two --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are we talking one or two more, or tens more, or hundreds more? Are you able to narrow it down to that?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's certainly not one or two. It's tens, at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, if you would have understood my questions well about the short range, you would have known that it's already implicit in my questions that if you would want to look at local communications for the whole of the area - and that's the comprehensive part of your question - of course that would require more. That there is no doubt about that -- there was no doubt in my mind, and I think it was already clear from the question. So it's -- my question was focussing very much on matters in certain areas rather than the comprehensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I just wanted to see if the witness could put a number on and I've finished. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Friedman, may I take it no further questions. Mr. Petrovic, no further questions. Then Mr. Vujovic, I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for answering the many questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench. I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher. And before the next witness enters the courtroom, I'd like to read a few decisions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness's microphone was off, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you switch -- yes, the microphone is on now. You said two or three words. In order not to miss anything, your microphone was switched off, so if you would repeat them so that we would know what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That is what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. To be quite honest, I recognise some of these words in B/C/S by now. Thank you very much. Please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the next witness be on standby. I would like to read two decisions. I'll start with the first one. The Chamber will now deliver its third decision on the "Stanisic Motion for Admission of Documents through the Bar Table." On the 17th of February, 2012, the Stanisic Defence requested the admission into evidence of 674 documents from the bar table. With leave of the Chamber, the Prosecution responded to the motion on the 23rd of March, 2012. The Simatovic Defence did not make any submissions in respect of the motion. On the 23rd of May, the Chamber issued its first decision on the motion, and stated that it would issue further decisions on the motion in due course. The Chamber hereby issues its fourth decision on the motion, which deals exclusively with the fourth category of documents contained in the second bar table chart, entitled: "RS MUP." These can be found in Confidential Annex B to the motion. The Stanisic Defence argues that the 61 documents contained in this category are highly probative and relevant to its case. For each of the documents in this category, the Prosecution has responded that it does not accept the conclusions the Stanisic Defence draws from these documents. Nonetheless, the Prosecution does not oppose their admission from the bar table. For many of the documents in Category 4, the Defence indicates that they support, and I quote, "the Defence position that any alleged assistance or support by the RDB or Jovica Stanisic to the RS MUP was nonexistent or insignificant, with other actors being the principal partners and suppliers," and that they are, and I again quote, "therefore probative of the lack of any significant contribution to the criminal objective or the crimes of the Bosnian Serbs by the RDB or Jovica Stanisic." For each document, the Defence has added a short explanation, sometimes accompanied by page references - of how the document tends to support the aforementioned proposition. While the aforementioned explanations and references were usually sufficient for the purpose of their admission from the bar table, the Chamber notes with concern that the descriptions and/or sparse references offered by the Defence for documents bearing Rule 65 ter numbers 1508, 2077, 1534, 1498, and 2216 offer little assistance as to which portions of these voluminous documents are relevant to the Defence case, thereby rendering the Chamber unable to properly assess the relevance and probative value. By way of example, the Chamber draws the attention to document bearing Rule 65 ter number 2077. Based on this sizable document, the Defence requests that the Chamber draws a broad negative inference, yet it offers only a scant description of its relevance to the Defence case, referencing a three-page section of a very lengthy report. The same can be said for document bearing Rule 65 ter number 1534, in relation to which the Defence seeks the Chamber to draw a similar broad negative inference, referencing 5 pages of a 58-page report. This report, in practice, is more a compilation of several reports covering various issues which, at first glance, appear to be of little relevance to the Defence case. Lastly, document bearing Rule 65 ter number 2216 is a lengthy interview with Momcilo Mandic published in the "Slobodna Bosna" in 1998, which only in part covers the purpose for which it is tendered. In sum, the Chamber concludes that for these documents the Defence has not fulfilled the requirements for their admission from the bar table. Accordingly, the Chamber denies their admission into evidence, without prejudice. Based on the submissions by the Stanisic Defence, and considering that the Prosecution does not oppose admission, the Chamber finds that the remaining 56 documents contained in Category 4 of the second bar table chart are probative and relevant. Moreover, the Stanisic Defence has demonstrated with clarity and specificity where and how each document fits into its case. Therefore, the Chamber grants the motion in this respect and admits these documents into evidence. Rather than reading out the document numbers here, the Registrar -- and the decision reads "has been handed a document," before I read that, I would like to hand out a document to the Registrar. The Registrar has by now been handed a document which references each of the 56 documents admitted, and the parties will receive copies at this very moment. The Chamber observes that a number of documents admitted have been introduced in order to show a negative, i.e., that something did not occur because the documents make no reference to it. As the Chamber stated in its earlier decisions on the motion, when such documents are tendered from the bar table, if viewed in isolation and without context provided by a tendering witness, there is a risk that less weight will ultimately be ascribed to them by the Chamber. In order to properly determine the weight of documents for which a negative inference is sought, the Chamber encourages the Defence by providing clear references to these documents in its final brief, to elaborate on the conclusions, if any, it invites the Chamber to draw from them collectively and/or individually, including, if appropriate, an explanation of how they refute the Prosecution evidence regarding the same issues. The Registry is requested to assign exhibit numbers to the documents admitted and inform the Chamber and the parties once it has done so. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. Then another decision of a rather technical nature. It is a decision amending the dead-line for the filing of public redacted versions of exhibits. The Chamber will now address the filing of public redacted versions of confidential exhibits. On the 23rd of August, 2010, the Chamber instructed the parties to submit, where possible, public redacted versions of the confidential exhibits they had tendered in a public filing. The Chamber set the dead-line for this filing to after the end of the presentation of evidence and at least two weeks before the filing of final briefs. Since August 2010, the Republic of Serbia has filed many requests for protective measures in relation to a large number of documents. Some of these requests are still pending. The Chamber therefore considers it appropriate to adjust the parties' dead-line for filing public redacted versions of confidential exhibits. The parties may commence such filings following the end of the presentation of evidence. The dead-line is set to eight weeks after the filing of final briefs. Should any motion for protective measures remain pending at the time of this dead-line, the Chamber will set a separate dead-line for filing public redacted versions in its decision on such a motion. And this concludes the Chamber's statement. Could the next witness be brought into the courtroom, unless there is any procedural matter. Yes. We'll start with the next witness, as we usually do, in private session. We move into private session and the witness may be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could you please make that solemn declaration, Mr. Micic. The text is in your hands now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Micic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Bakrac is counsel for Mr. Simatovic. You'll find him over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Micic. Mr. Micic, before we start putting our questions, we always caution our witnesses who speak the same language that we do, they should pause between my question and the answer that they are about to give so that the interpreters could interpret both the question and answer correctly. So please answer once I've finished my question, and, if possible, could you try to speak slower so that your answers could be followed properly. So now I'm going to start dealing with certain things that we always deal with for the benefit of the transcript. Please give us your full name and surname.

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE MICIC
utterances.text: Radivoje Micic. Father's name, Sredoje.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind as to tell us your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE MICIC
utterances.text: A very long time ago, the 14th of December, 1958.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Our age is similar, Mr. Micic, and therefore I would not agree that it was that long ago, but let's move on. Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE MICIC
utterances.text: In Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what your profession is?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE MICIC
utterances.text: I have a degree in law, and once I passed the bar exam, then I completed my training in that way. That was in the late 1980s.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And can you tell us what your profession is right now?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE MICIC
utterances.text: Right now I am a retiree. I've been retired for a very long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me when you got your law degree and when?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE MICIC
utterances.text: In 1985 in Belgrade, the University of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: After you got your law degree, what was the first job you had?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE MICIC
utterances.text: Briefly, I was involved in legal affairs at the Sopot municipality, which is one of the suburbs of Belgrade. That was for about nine and a half months. After that I got a job with the Ministry of the Interior, the SDB, the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, briefly, when you were admitted into the State Security Service and, again briefly, what your career was there up until 1991, and then I will put a few specific questions to you in relation to the work you did.

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE MICIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of January, 1987, I started my employment with the DB. I was a trainee for a year. And then in the beginning of 1988, I started working in the American group of the Belgrade centre of the then state security sector of the security service. I worked as an operative, as one usually does when starting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So in 1991 --

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE MICIC
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: -- what is the position you held, and what did you do specifically?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE MICIC
utterances.text: In 1991, that job was called "operative." Just that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: As an operative, were you posted in a particular organisational unit?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE MICIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, from the very beginning I became part of the American group. That was 1988.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: This American group, did it have some abbreviation that it was known by, and if so, what was it?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE MICIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was AOS. It was the AOS group within the centre of the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: -- and in the beginning of 1992, who was the head of your group?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE MICIC
utterances.text: At that time, it was still Mr. Franko Simatovic. When I say "at that time," I'm saying that he was the head of that group. So basically I think that he must have been the head even before I joined the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say "head of the group," can you tell us from an organisational point of view what was the level at the SDB or the RDB, at which organisational level was that group?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE MICIC
utterances.text: That was the lowest organisational level, if I can put it that way. There was nothing else. There was no organisation below that, so freely speaking we can say that this was a group of operatives that had a particular job. So this was the smallest organisational entity with a particular task.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You say "with a particular task." Could you please be so kind as to tell us what were the tasks of this American group that you belonged to?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE MICIC
utterances.text: Counter-intelligence at the time. In the most general possible terms, if it is possible to define this, it would go as follows: Intelligence vis-a-vis the American community, registration, and stopping or preventing intelligence activities by the American community.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, it just seems to me that there is some difference between the transcript and what you said. So I am going to ask you to repeat what you said. So what is the subject of interest?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE MICIC
utterances.text: First of all, the activity of the American Intelligence Services, or, rather, community, because there is more than seven of them. It varied. That's as far as activity goes. As far as activity is concerned, it has to do with registering that activity, establishing what it is and with a view to stopping it, whatever that may mean; that is to say, stopping the intelligence work of a foreign intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you share with us some of the examples of tasks you were involved in in 1991?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE MICIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, my tasks were directly linked with some names. I countered some activities, and my starting point was preliminary processing. If I gave you examples, I would also have to give you some very specific names.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Unless the Trial Chamber insists on the names, I am just interested in the categories of those individuals that you processed.

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE MICIC
utterances.text: At first that was called the operative investigation of American interns who resided in Yugoslavia and primarily in Belgrade, because our centre was in Belgrade, as well as our own interns who went for the purpose of continuing education to the United States of America. Also within the scope of my work and duties were American journalists who stayed in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us something about the work of the group and the activities that you were involved in? Who was your co-ordinator? Who co-ordinated all that?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE MICIC
utterances.text: The person immediately in charge of co-ordination, advising, and supervision was the head of the group, and later on things changed and that person who was head of group or the group leader became the head of section. That was Mr. Simatovic during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, the group leader who later on became the head of section, who did he report to and who he received his assignments from?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE MICIC
utterances.text: The organisation followed a vertical subordination, and at that time it was the assistant chief of the department in the centre of the RDB and also the chief of department. Again, following a certain line of subordination, higher up it was the chief of the Belgrade centre. That would be above the immediate superior line along that same vertical line.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, let's just explain for the record. When you said that you followed a vertical line of subordination, at that time it was the assistant head of department in the RDB centre.

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Which RDB?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE MICIC
utterances.text: The RDB in Belgrade. All this time I've been talking about Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Micic.

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE MICIC
utterances.text: I apologise, just a moment, please. Whatever I am sharing with you is very strictly confidential. It's a state secret, so I don't know whether I should be telling you this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, we already had experts who testified about that and I believe that your testimony so far may be made available to the general public. Do you know or can you estimate how many members did your group have?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE MICIC
